en: 7. The Chapter on the Pairs of Latent Tendencies (Anusayayamaka) 7.2 The Major Section (Mahāvāra) 7.2.3 The Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra)
7.2.3.1. Positive Person (Anulomapuggala) Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust also abandons the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.
Or rather, is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to aversion also abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.
He who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust also abandons the underlying tendency to conceit?
He abandons that which is associated with it.
Or, he who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit also abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust also abandoning the underlying tendency to views … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
Or rather, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust?
One abandons that which is associated with it.
Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust abandoning the underlying tendency to existence … pe … abandoning the underlying tendency to ignorance?
One abandons that which is associated with it.
Or else, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
He who abandons the underlying tendency to aversion also abandons the underlying tendency to conceit?
He abandons that which is associated with it.
Or, he who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit also abandons the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to aversion also abandoning the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt?
No. Or rather, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt also abandoning the underlying tendency to aversion?
One abandons that which is associated with it.
Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to aversion abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance?
One abandons that which is associated with it.
Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance abandon the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also abandoning the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)… [and so on] …the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?
No. Or rather, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt also abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit?
One abandons that which is associated with it (tadekaṭṭha).
He who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or rather, he who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance abandons the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
He who abandons the underlying tendency to views abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or again, does he who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt abandon the underlying tendency to views? Yes.
… [as before] … Does he who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance?
He abandons that which is associated with it.
Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence also abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes. (End of the section based on a single root.)
Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit?
One abandons that which is associated with them.
Or, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion abandon the underlying tendency to views … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt?

No. Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? One abandons those [tendencies] associated with that [abandonment].
Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also abandon the underlying tendency to existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance?
One abandons that which is associated with them.
Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? No. (The Section Based on Pairs.)
Is he who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also abandoning the underlying tendency to views ... pe ...

the underlying tendency to doubt? No. Or else, is he who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit? He abandons those [tendencies] associated with that [state].

Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also abandoning the underlying tendency to existence ... pe ... the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.
Or else, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
One abandons the underlying tendency to conceit. (End of the section based on the Triad.)

Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, also abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? No.

Or else, is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to doubt also abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views?

One who abandons the underlying tendency to views abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, as well as those factors associated with them... [etc. (End of the Section Based on Fourfold Roots).

Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, also abandoning the underlying tendency to existence … pe … the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?
[He] abandons the underlying tendency to conceit. (The section based on the pentad.)

Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, also abandoning the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or else, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence?
One abandons the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to lust for existence. (The Sixfold Root.)

7.2.3.2. Positive Section (Anuloma-okāsa) Is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Or rather, is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Or rather, is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit there, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust there. In the sense-sphere element, with respect to two types of feeling, one abandons both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

Is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or rather, is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

From the feeling of pain, and from the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, but one does not [abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust].

From that, one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust. In two feelings within the sense-sphere realm, from that [feeling], one abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is it the case that from whatever [feeling] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, from that same [feeling] one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence? No.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure? No.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure?
In the unpleasant feeling, in the form element, and in the formless element, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance,

but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one abandons both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or rather, is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or rather, is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt there, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion there.
In the feeling of pain (dukkhā vedanā), one abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and [the underlying tendency to aversion] there.
One abandons the underlying tendency to aversion.
Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence? No.
Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or conversely, is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the fine-material and immaterial realms (rūpadhātu and arūpadhātu), one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance [but not necessarily the underlying tendency to aversion].

And yet, one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) by that [feeling]. In regard to painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), one abandons both the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), there one also abandons the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? Yes, it is so.
Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit?
In regard to painful feeling, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt there, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to conceit there.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), one abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and [the underlying tendency to conceit].
One abandons the underlying tendency to conceit. Is it the case that because one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence there. In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), one abandons both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit?
In regard to painful feeling, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance therefrom, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to conceit therefrom.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms (rūpadhātu and arūpadhātu), one abandons both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to conceit therefrom.
Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to views, one also abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to views? Yes.
… [as before] … Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence?
In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt there, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence there.
He abandons them. From the fine-material element or the immaterial element, he abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Or, from whatever [plane] he abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, from that same [plane] does he abandon the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
From whatever [plane] he abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, from that same [plane] does he abandon the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) therefrom, but does not abandon the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) therefrom.
In the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial realm (*arūpadhātu*), one abandons both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to lust for existence therefrom.
(Based on a single root.)
Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or rather, is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit there, but one does not [abandon] the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion there.

And he abandons the underlying tendency to aversion. In two feelings of the sense-sphere realm, one abandons the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.

Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to views ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt? No.
Or, when one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, does one thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt therefrom, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.
In the sense-sphere element, in two types of feeling, one abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust therefrom.

One abandons [the latent tendency of ignorance], but one does not abandon the latent tendency of aversion from that same state. In regard to painful feeling, one abandons both the latent tendency of doubt and the latent tendency of aversion, but one does not abandon the latent tendency of sensual lust from that same state.

Is it the case that wherever one abandons both the latent tendency of sensual lust and the latent tendency of aversion, one also abandons the latent tendency of attachment to existence from that same state? No.

Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons both the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure and the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Is it the case that when one abandons both the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure and the underlying tendency to aversion, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance?

There is no such case. Or is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons both the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance therefrom, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one abandons both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to sensual lust therefrom, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.
In the feeling of pain, one [abandons] the underlying tendency to ignorance therefrom...
One abandons the underlying tendency to aversion, but one does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust. (End of the section based on pairs.

Is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to views …pe… the underlying tendency to doubt? No.

Or rather, is it the case that from whatever [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, from that same [plane] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion. In painful [feeling]...

From feeling, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion, but one does not abandon from there the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit.

Is it the case that from whatever [feeling] one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to existence? No.
Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit?
One abandons the underlying tendency to conceit.
Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or rather, when one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), does one thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), and the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*)?

In the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*), one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion. In the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), in two types of feeling, one [abandons] the underlying tendency to ignorance...
One abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to aversion from that state.

In painful feeling, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to aversion from that state, but one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit from that state.
(End of the section based on triplets.)

Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, there one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, there one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views.
And yet, one does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm, one abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, but one does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to aversion. In painful feeling, one [abandons] the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion.
One abandons the underlying tendency to views, but one does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit … (End of the section based on four.

Is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, there one abandons the underlying tendency to existence? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one abandons the underlying tendency to existence, there one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?

One abandons the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt. Is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that whenever one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt;

yet one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therein. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element, one [abandons] the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt.
One abandons [the latent tendency of ignorance], but does not abandon the latent tendency of aversion from that state.

In painful feeling, one abandons the latent tendencies of ignorance, aversion, views, and doubt from that state, but does not abandon the latent tendencies of sensual lust and conceit from that state. (The pentad-based section.)

Is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that when one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, one thereby abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence; yet one does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therefrom.

In the sensual element, within two types of feeling, one [abandons] the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views therefrom.
One abandons the underlying tendency to doubt, but does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

In regard to painful feeling, one abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, but does not thereby abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence. (The Sixfold Rooted Set.)

7.2.3.3. Positive Person-Space (Anuloma-Puggalokāsa) Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) from a particular [plane] also abandons the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) from that same plane? No.
Or rather, is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to aversion from a particular plane also abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust from that same plane? No.

Is one who abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to a certain object also abandoning the underlying tendency to conceit with respect to that same object? One abandons it as part of that same category (*tadekaṭṭha*).
Or, is one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit with respect to a certain object also abandoning the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to that same object? No.

Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) from a particular [plane] also abandons the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) from that same plane?
No. Or rather, is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from a particular plane also abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust from that same plane?

The person in the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*)—in relation to painful feeling, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*arūpadhātu*)—abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from those planes, but does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

And yet, he does not abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) because of that. That same person, in two types of feeling within the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), abandons the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) and abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust along with its associated states.

Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to sensual lust from a certain state also abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) from that same state? No.

Or again, is he who abandons the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) from a certain plane thereby abandoning the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure (kāmarāgānusaya)? No.
Is he who abandons the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure from a certain plane thereby abandoning the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?
He abandons that which is associated with it (tadekaṭṭha).

Or rather, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) from that same plane? No.
Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) from that same plane? No.
Or rather, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to aversion from that same plane? No.

Is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) from a certain [plane] also abandons the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) from that same plane?
No. Or rather, is it the case that whoever abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from a certain plane also abandons the underlying tendency to aversion from that same plane?

The person in the eighth stage (*aṭṭhamaka*)—in the two feelings of the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*), and in the fine-material sphere (*rūpadhātu*) and immaterial sphere (*arūpadhātu*)—abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from those planes.

He abandons [the latent tendency to ignorance], yet he does not abandon the latent tendency to aversion from that state. That same person, in regard to painful feeling, abandons the latent tendency to doubt and abandons the latent tendency to aversion along with its associated factors.
Is it the case that whoever abandons the latent tendency to aversion from a certain state also abandons the latent tendency to attachment to existence from that state? No.

Or again, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) from a particular plane also abandon the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) from that same plane? No.
Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to aversion from a particular plane also abandon the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) from that same plane?
One abandons it as part of that same category (tadekaṭṭha).
Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) from that same plane? No.

Does one who abandons the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)… [and] the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) from that same plane? No.
Or, does one who abandons the underlying tendency to doubt from a certain plane also abandon the underlying tendency to conceit from that same plane? No.
The person at the eighth stage, in regard to painful feeling, abandons the underlying tendency to doubt therefrom, but does not abandon the underlying tendency to conceit therefrom.
That same person, in regard to the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm and in regard to the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms,
abandons the underlying tendency to doubt therefrom and abandons the underlying tendency to conceit that is associated therewith.
